prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, reaching unprecedented accuracy and stability in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: My own opening first choice, B036 (defect-mediated 2D melting and the hexatic phase), attracted no support from any colleague, and that is information I should weigh rather than dismiss. On re-reading the shortlist I find the optical lattice clock the strongest case on the criteria I actually apply: a simple, general mechanism, a clean attribution, and demonstrated agreement between theory and measurement. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift as a systematic, which is an elegant piece of physics rather than only engineering. Ye's group then pushed the clocks to the 1e-18 level and into many-body regimes, with independent confirmation across JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE. The two-name credit is clean, five members already rank it in their top three, and it opens genuinely new measurements: tests of constants, searches for dark matter, and relativistic geodesy. As someone who cares whether a result is understood and not only whether it works, I note that every systematic in these clocks is understood in quantitative detail, which is rare for a field this young.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is novelty relative to the 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch, frequency combs, with Ye working in that lineage) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, control of single quantum systems). A critic can read the lattice clock as a refinement of a metrological chain already honoured. There is also a timing argument: the SI second has not yet been redefined, and Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and others made substantial contributions that a two-name prize leaves out. Separately, my own B036 and the B042 moire case both have the advantage that they would reward conceptual physics rather than instrumentation, and I do not want to let a preference for what is easy to attribute crowd out what is deep.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B046 first because lattice clocks are the most precise measuring instruments ever built and open new observation channels, with a clean two-name credit.
responses.response: I largely agree on the science and attribution, and I accept that the redefinition of the second does not need to be settled for the science to be mature. My qualification is that precision alone is not the argument; what persuades me is that the magic-wavelength mechanism is a simple idea whose consequences are quantitatively understood. I would press you on the 2005 overlap, since Ye already shares that prize: I think the committee should state in the citation that the new element is the lattice trapping and the many-body clock, not the comb.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B038 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) first as a verified theory-to-experiment chain that created a new class of quantum matter, and B042 second.
responses.response: I respect the B038 case on importance and stable interpretation, but I do not rank it above B046. The topological-insulator story follows the 2016 prize on topological phases, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, which made the Molenkamp experiment possible, is outside the supplied credit, so the three names give an incomplete account of who first identified the mechanism. I do agree with you that B042 deserves serious weight; where we differ is that you treat the unsettled superconducting mechanism as a lesser concern, while I think it argues for waiting a few years.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B046 first and sees it as atomic physics at its most precise, where theory and experiment agree quantitatively, while noting the neighbouring 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with your reading that the 2005 and 2012 prizes cover neighbouring ground but not this invention. Your comment that the topological-insulator line to the 2016 prize may be debated is, I think, the right test for B038 as well as for my own B036, and I accept that the same overlap objection applies to my first choice. I would add that your remark about Lemonde and others means the citation should be worded around the invention of the lattice clock and its realization, not the whole field.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B051 (WMAP) first, but places B042 fourth, calling the Bistritzer-MacDonald-Jarillo-Herrero trio clean while judging the field somewhat early.
responses.response: We agree that B042 is a clean attribution and a striking theory-experiment pairing, and I share your concern about maturity, since the nature of the superconducting and correlated states is still debated. I rank it higher than you do because the continuum-model argument is compact and universal. But I would not make it the preferred prize now for exactly the reason you give, which is why I list it as an alternative. On B051 I would ask whether a third cosmology recognition after COBE and Peebles is the best use of a prize, given the redundancy you acknowledge yourself.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will read the lattice clock as new relative to the 2005 comb and 2012 prizes, given that Ye already shares the 2005 prize.
Whether a two-name credit for Katori and Ye adequately reflects Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and others, and whether to wait for the SI second redefinition.

Whether B036 is covered by the 2016 prize and whether the hexatic scenario is universal enough, given system-dependent first-order behaviour; my recollection of the Young, Halperin, Nelson and Kosterlitz-Thouless priority history is from memory and not checked.
Whether the unsettled pairing mechanism makes B042 premature.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I am at the University of Gothenburg, in the same physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson at Chalmers, but I have found no collaboration with them or with any shortlisted candidate. My own first-choice candidate B036 has no known link to me.
